items.title: Jev in Java and Spring Boot (It's Not an LLM)
items.description:
Here is a support message from someone who is losing sales. Run it, and three answers come back. Is it urgent? A probability. Which team? A choice. How bad? A score with a confidence. All in about a hundred milliseconds. No prompt. No chat. No parsing a paragraph of JSON. This is Jev. It is not an LLM. There is no official Java SDK, and that does not matter.

This is a getting started guide to Jev from TypeSafe for Java and Spring developers. First we cover what Jev is and is not at a high level, including the three primitives and where it fits. Then we make the same call from plain Java 25 in one file, and then again from Spring Boot 4 with a RestClient and records.

- What Jev is and what it is not: typed decisions with a probability and a confidence, not generated text
- The three primitives you work with: noul, choice, and score
- Why Jev has no official Java SDK and why that does not matter (it is one HTTP endpoint)
- How to call Jev from plain Java 25 in one file with no framework and no dependencies
- How to build the same call in Spring Boot 4 with a RestClient and records, the version to keep

If you learned something, click like and subscribe, and drop a comment if you want the YouTube comment moderation build next.

0:00 - Intro: one message in, three typed answers out
0:48 - What is Jev?
4:34 - What people are building with Jev
11:11 - Console, playground, and docs
14:41 - Plain Java 25 example (one file, no SDK)
18:55 - Spring Boot 4 with a RestClient
22:30 - Run and read the typed answers

items.title: Total Recall: Agent Memory and Harness Engineering — Ignacio Martinez, Oracle
items.description:
Ignacio Martinez registered the domain for this workshop on the Saturday before he gave it, and then asked the room not to request the biggest machines on offer, because he was paying for everyone's GitHub Codespace out of his own pocket. That improvisation sits oddly beside the argument underneath it, which is one of the more carefully built cases for harness engineering here. A language model, he says, is the frozen part of the reasoning. The weights do not change, you rent them, and you have no say in what you are offered. Everything you control lives in the layer around it. So an agent is a model plus a harness, and harness engineering is the work of turning a nondeterministic core into repeatable output.

He builds that harness in seven layers, and the sharpest arguments are about where memory physically lives. Files match a model's instincts and cost nothing to append to, but they have no transactional consistency, which is why, when he asks the room how parallel agents avoid trampling each other, the answer comes back immediately: work trees. Databases solved that a long time ago, he notes, and everyone forgot. His semantic layer borrows Umwelt from the biologist Jakob von Uexküll, whose claim was that every organism perceives reality only through the lens it happens to have. An agent's lens is whatever institutional knowledge you remembered to write down. Two ideas stay with you. A hysteresis variable encoding how much patience the harness extends to the model before it gives up on a task. And skill promotion, where a workflow that cost you four hours is distilled into a better version and the original retired.

items.title: Virtual Threads Aren't Enough: Structured Concurrency in Java 27
items.description:
Virtual threads made this method twice as fast. They did nothing to make it safe. Flip one flag, the user service fails after 200ms, and the version built on virtual threads and Futures still runs for a full second for a result nobody will use.

We build the same loadDashboard method three times: sequential, then virtual threads with Future, then StructuredTaskScope. You will see exactly where the Future version wastes work when a call fails, and how the scope cancels the sibling call in 200ms instead of a full second. This is built on the JDK 27 API (JEP 533) that JDK 28 plans to make final.

- Why virtual threads plus Future have no lifetime link to the method that started them
- How a failed call leaves the other call running and wasting a full second of work
- How StructuredTaskScope groups related tasks into one unit that fails or finishes together
- The JDK 27 shape: open(), fork(), join() and the new checked ExecutionException
- Why JDK 26 tutorials no longer compile, and how to run with --enable-preview

If this helped, leave a thumbs up and subscribe. As always, happy coding.

0:00 - The one-flag failure demo
1:00 - JDK 27 and the JEP list
2:30 - What is structured concurrency
3:30 - Project Loom: virtual threads, scoped values, structured concurrency
5:30 - Sequential version: simple but slow
7:30 - Parallel version: virtual threads + Future
9:30 - The problem: a Future has no lifetime relationship
10:30 - Structured version: open, fork, join
12:30 - The JDK 27 API change: checked ExecutionException
13:30 - Flip the flag: 200ms vs a full second
14:30 - Wrap up and what's next

items.title: I Built the App That Runs My YouTube Channel With Claude Code
items.description:
Every video on this channel now goes through this app. I built it. Well, I built it with Claude Code. 309 commits and 80,000 lines of code. Eight months ago I wrote in my newsletter that this would have taken me ten times longer. And here is the part that still feels a little scary. Claude does not just build this app. It uses it.

This is a tour of Content OS, the app I open every morning to run every video, blog post, newsletter, podcast, and talk. It is a real Spring Boot app I built with Claude Code over eight months, and I use it every day. I will walk you through the features, show you the code and the MCP server, and share why I am more excited to be a builder right now than ever.

- Why AI made a project exist that never would have been worth building before
- How a project moves through a 16-stage pipeline from raw idea to published newsletter
- How a video transcript turns into a blog post companion for the site
- How the MCP server lets Claude work inside the app from the terminal
- The real stack behind it: Java, Spring Boot 4, Spring AI, JTE, and PostgreSQL

If this inspired you to build your own tool, leave a thumbs up, subscribe to the channel, and tell me in the comments what you would build. Happy coding.

0:00 - The app that runs my whole channel

items.title: Homa: The End of TCP for AI Clusters — John Ousterhout, Stanford
items.description:
John Ousterhout, Stanford Professor and author of A Philosophy of Software Design, turns our attention to the evolving nature of AI networking workloads and why traditional protocols like TCP and RDMA are becoming bottlenecks in modern data center environments!

The Shift in Workloads

Historical context: AI traffic was dominated by massive, long-running transfers (gigabytes of gradients), where throughput was the primary metric (2:19-2:42).
Modern AI: Workloads, especially inference and agentic applications, now rely on frequent, small coordination messages (e.g., KV cache lookups, barrier synchronization). These small messages are highly sensitive to latency (3:09-4:02).
The Bottleneck: When small synchronization messages are mixed with large traffic, they get trapped in queues (caused by incast), significantly increasing 99th percentile (tail) latency. This causes GPUs to sit idle, wasting expensive compute resources (4:24-5:34).
Why Legacy Protocols Struggle
Sender-Driven Congestion Control: TCP and RDMA rely on the sender to detect congestion, often via packet drops or delayed signals from switches. This process is inherently reactive and oscillates, leading to unstable performance (7:10-9:58).
Byte Stream Model: These protocols view data as an opaque stream of bytes rather than discrete messages, making it difficult to prioritize short, critical tasks (10:05-11:05).

The Homa Solution

John introduces Homa, a clean-slate transport protocol designed for data centers (11:15-12:15):
Message-Based: Unlike byte streams, Homa understands message boundaries, allowing it to predict traffic and prioritize short messages using Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) (12:22-13:28).
Receiver-Driven: The receiver controls the flow by issuing grants to senders, effectively managing congestion before it occurs at the switch (13:30-14:58).

items.title: I Publish My Podcast with Claude Code and Skills
items.description:
This is the raw recording from the Spring Office Hours episode I finished an hour ago. Before it goes out, four things have to happen: edit the audio, write the show notes, publish it, and open a PR on the spring.io blog. Same four steps, every episode, for years. Today I'm not doing any of them by hand. Skills are. And here's the part most people miss: not one of them writes code.

In this video I use four Claude Code skills to take one raw podcast recording all the way to a published episode. You will see what a skill really is, when to reach for one, and a real live run: edit the audio, generate show notes, publish to Transistor, and open a PR on the spring.io blog.

- What a skill actually is: a folder with a markdown file of instructions, sometimes with a script
- When to reach for a skill: the second time you do something by hand
- Where skills sit between doing it yourself and pushing a button
- How four skills carry a raw recording to an mp3, a transcript, a clipboard description, and a spring.io PR

items.title: AI Skills with Matt Pocock
items.description:
Why is the “grill-me” skill so popular, and why does its creator swear by the importance of software fundamentals? Matt Pocock created this widely-used skill – and many others – alongside being an educator, content creator, and engineer. His latest course is AI Hero, and he previously created the Total TypeScript course that generated more than $2.5 million in sales.

In this episode, Matt and I discuss his unconventional path from working as a voice teacher to becoming a developer and going all-in on technical education. He reveals how communication skills helped him break into tech, why he took an unusual three-days-a-week contract at Vercel, and how he built Total TypeScript through workshops, courses, and a lot of free content.

We also explore “strategic coding,” and how he uses skills like “grill me” and “wayfinder” to plan, delegate, and course-correct with AI agents. Matt explains his “day shift” and “night shift” approach, why splitting context up can keep agents in their “smart zone,” and how concepts from classic software engineering books can guide agents to do better. In this episode, there’s also local versus cloud workflows, whether agents need TDD, how AI is changing the ways that engineers learn the fundamentals, and why humans are still essential in teaching.
